Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB212.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Eryin Mi. At the lantern festival, Eryin Mi describes dragon lanterns colliding, fireworks scattering blossoms and fire striking faces so painfully that even Shakyamuni feels it. Where is the ancient Buddha Dipamkara, whose name evokes a lamp, at this very moment? Eryin answers with a drunken crowd shoulder to shoulder, helping one another home at midnight amid pipes and singing. The exact pair supplies a festive bodily scene in response to the Buddha question. It is a poetic cap within the address, not a report that the master or assembly became drunk or a directive that drinking is the way to find a Buddha.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB276.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Buhui. Buhui Fatong gives the pair at a full-moon festival address requested by a military patron honoring his parents and praying for a descendant. Dragon lanterns, fire, a wooden boy clapping and a stone woman playing pipes lead into gratitude and hearing turned back toward its nature. Raising his whisk, he asks where Avalokiteshvara dwells and answers with revelers supporting each other home. He then challenges another old exchange about seeing Manjushri. The crowded homecoming is his present answer within this ritual setting; the source does not decode drunkenness itself as a particular attainment or establish actual wine drinking by the people gathered.

The institutional chamber where direct examination and private interviews occur, not merely any room interior. Tianyi Yihuai questions an unnamed monk in the chamber (室中問僧); other masters present old sayings there or arrange an object and test each entrant. Dahui Zonggao's biography says he was assigned to share the chamber seat and “grasp the bamboo switch to test students” (令分座室中，握竹篦以騐學者); Xiaoweng Miaokan repeatedly presents the no-buddha-nature saying there and strikes when the student begins to speak. Recorded-sayings collections can therefore label a section “chamber encounters” (室中機緣). The word names the location and institutional setting, not the student's entrance: “enter the chamber for an interview” (入室) names the entrance, whereas “in the chamber” (室中) names the setting. Nor does the setting itself certify approval or succession.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count across both senses: 1,566 hits in 274 texts. Distinct technical deployments preserved here are a direct chamber question, delegated examination by a head monk, presentation of a named old saying, an arranged-object test for entrants, and the section label “chamber encounters.” The Zen bend is the chamber's repeated use as an interview and testing setting.

Senses.Explanation: In ordinary spatial narration, the headword simply means “inside a room” (室中). Shiqi Tongyun writes, “idle inside the room, I cannot be bothered to burn incense” (室中無事懶燒香); Tianyin Yuanxiu describes someone “lying ill in a single room” (臥病一室中). Senses.PreferredTarget: A vast marsh can hide a mountain; fitting principle can subdue a leopard.
AlternateTargets: Broad waters conceal a mountain; sound judgment can tame a leopard.
SearchAliases: vast marsh hides mountain principle tames leopard
Senses.Note: The pair joins a vast marsh hiding a mountain with principle or apt handling that can overcome a fierce leopard. In the older bench case Xuedou voices it; repeated records carry that source. Linye, Shenfeng, and Guantao use it as the close of their own present instruction. Yikui acknowledges it while arguing that an immediate blow would have been sharper. The image praises capacity, but the current uses also test its limits.

Senses.Explanation: The first clause imagines a marsh broad enough to conceal a mountain; the second imagines sound principle or apt handling overcoming a leopard. Senses.Note: The scriptural line says coarse words and subtle speech both return to the highest meaning. Linquan cites it while rejecting a simplistic silence. Guxue quotes his teacher after a staged objection that ordinary affairs are only worldly talk. Zhenxie applies it to rough speech in a village, and Baiyu turns the line into another question about which meaning his impossible images belong to.

Senses.Explanation: ‘Coarse words and fine speech alike return to the ultimate meaning’ is a scriptural line that later masters use against a rigid division of speech into high and low kinds. They still ask whether the listener can meet the point in a present talk. Linquan cites the scripture while warning that trying to take refuge in silence can also miss the matter. Guxue cites his teacher after a staged objection that his ordinary almanac talk has no place in a hall sermon. Zhenxie gives the line and uses village quarrels as rough speech that still calls for thorough seeing. Baiyu opens with the line, describes impossible acts, and asks the audience which meaning they belong to.

Senses.Explanation: Coarse words and fine speech names the rough and refined ends of spoken expression together. Zhongfeng Mingben says that, for someone with actual realization, not only learned discourse but coarse words, fine speech, wind, and rain accord with Bodhidharma's Chan. Zhe'an Jingfan says his monastery neither investigates mysteries nor deals in coarse words and fine speech, but has spent successive days harvesting. Gufeng Dexiu's verse says coarse words and fine speech do not concern the person in question. Danyun Qingjing calls his own hall talk unstudied speech blurted out as coarse words and fine speech. Yulin Tongxiu's biographer says that all his coarse words and fine speech lodged a significance beyond the words' surface.
